title: DLP-LoRA: Efficient Task-Specific LoRA Fusion with a Dynamic, Lightweight Plugin for Large Language Models

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to enable dynamic, context-driven fusion of multiple task-specific LoRAs without manual pre-selection or retraining when tasks change, while remaining lightweight and adaptable to new domains. Paper [1] ("LoRA-Flow") shares a similar objective of dynamically combining LoRAs for new tasks, emphasizing reusability and adaptability. Paper [4] ("LoraHub") also targets dynamic LoRA composition for cross-task generalization, aiming to fluidly combine LoRAs for unseen tasks. Paper [5] ("LoraRetriever") addresses input-aware LoRA retrieval and composition for diverse tasks, which aligns with the goal of dynamic fusion without manual pre-selection. These papers collectively cover the purpose at the problem-class level.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves DLP-LoRA, a dynamic lightweight plugin (4-layer mini-MLP module, ~5M parameters) trained once for sentence-level task classification, which selects and fuses multiple LoRAs using top-p sampling strategies. Paper [1] ("LoRA-Flow") employs dynamic LoRA fusion but relies on task-level weights rather than sentence-level classification or top-p sampling. Paper [4] ("LoraHub") introduces a framework for dynamic LoRA composition but does not use a mini-MLP or top-p sampling. Paper [5] ("LoraRetriever") uses input-aware retrieval and composition but does not employ the same mechanism (mini-MLP trained for sentence-level classification with top-p sampling). None of the prior papers describe a substantively equivalent mechanism.

### Evaluation
The evaluation compares the plugin's parameter count (~5M) against a typical token-level gating method (~26M) on LLaMA-3 8B with 100 LoRAs, trained once at the sentence level. Paper [1] ("LoRA-Flow") evaluates dynamic LoRA fusion methods but does not use the same evaluation design (sentence-level training or parameter comparison). Paper [4] ("LoraHub") evaluates LoRA composition for unseen tasks but does not focus on parameter efficiency comparisons or sentence-level training. Paper [5] ("LoraRetriever") evaluates input-aware LoRA composition but does not use the same evaluation design. None of the prior papers employ the same evaluation design, making this facet uncovered.

### Domain
The domain is parameter-efficient fine-tuning and multi-task LLM adaptation. Papers [1], [4], and [5] all operate in the same general application area of parameter-efficient fine-tuning and multi-task LLM adaptation, even though they target different specific sub-problems or approaches. This facet is covered.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to reduce inference-time overhead caused by multi-LoRA fusion, particularly addressing inefficiencies from token-level MoE gating (e.g., MeteoRA). Paper [5] ("MeteoRA") explicitly identifies the same problem of token-level routing inflating inference costs, stating: "requires explicit task intention selection, posing challenges for autonomous task sensing and switching during inference with multiple existing LoRA adapters embedded in a single LLM." This aligns with the same objective of mitigating overhead from token-level routing in multi-LoRA setups.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves sentence-level LoRA selection and fusion, leveraging parallel CUDA acceleration and GEMM optimization by removing per-token independence constraints, with LoRAs stored as contiguous tensors in HBM. Paper [7] ("LoRA-Switch") describes a similar system-algorithm co-design approach to reduce latency in dynamic LoRA adapters, including addressing fragmented CUDA kernel inefficiencies. Additionally, paper [13] ("Flexible Performant GEMM Kernels on GPUs") discusses GEMM optimization techniques for efficient matrix operations on GPUs, which aligns with the GEMM optimization aspect of the mechanism. Both papers cover the underlying technical primitives used here.

### Evaluation
The evaluation demonstrates achieving less than twice the inference time of single-LoRA inference, outperforming token-level MoE gating routers in efficiency. Paper [5] ("MeteoRA") evaluates token-level MoE gating routers in terms of inference efficiency, and paper [7] ("LoRA-Switch") evaluates dynamic LoRA adapters with a focus on inference latency reduction. Both use similar evaluation designs, including latency benchmarks and comparisons against token-level routing methods. Thus, the evaluation design is covered.

### Domain
The domain is efficient LLM inference. Papers [1] ("A Survey on Efficient Inference for Large Language Models") and [12] ("LLM Inference Unveiled") both explicitly focus on efficient LLM inference as their application area, covering this domain. Paper [5] ("MeteoRA") also operates within the same domain, addressing efficient inference for multi-LoRA setups.
